summary:
New Brunswick sets its own schools policy and its own human rights rules inside the Canadian legal framework; criminal law and the national human rights statute sit with the federal government. The province's schools policy on sexual orientation and gender identity, issued by the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development, has been in force since 17 August 2020 and was revised on 1 July 2023, 23 August 2023 and 1 January 2025.

In the version effective 1 January 2025, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them in informal school settings, with parental consent encouraged but not required. Formal records for students under 16 still require parental consent.

The policy's application clause covers the school environment as a whole. Alongside students it names school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors, so a visitor who steps into a New Brunswick classroom falls within its rules.

Between 1 July 2023 and 31 December 2024 the policy barred teachers from using a student under 16's chosen name and pronouns without parental consent. That revision reversed a three-year-old requirement that teachers obtain the student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents, and it dropped explicit wording permitting students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity.

The policy as adopted in 2020 requires schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and to provide gender-neutral bathrooms.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodation is prohibited in New Brunswick, with gender identity and expression listed as prohibited grounds in the province's human rights legislation.
tangentialFactors:
The 2023 revision was made by executive policy without a legislative vote, the government citing complaints from parents and teachers. Two ministers resigned in protest and two others were removed; eight governing-party members, including six cabinet ministers, sat out question period to protest the lack of process and transparency, and party dissidents called for a leadership review. The national prime minister said trans kids in New Brunswick "need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians".

About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 against the review of the policy. A schools advocate who helped draft the 2020 policy said "we know it saves lives" and warned that "with this policy changed or removed, we're going to lose kids". The education minister confirmed the review was under way.

The revision announced in December 2024, effective 1 January 2025, goes beyond the recommendations of the provincial child advocate and undoes the 2023 consent rule, which had drawn protests and a constitutional challenge from a national civil-liberties group.

New Brunswick's 2023 rule was imposed by policy rather than statute. Two other provinces legislated comparable parental-consent requirements for students under 16 in 2023 and 2024 and shielded them with a constitutional override, and those measures drew legal challenges in their own courts.
localsOnly:
For residents, a student under 16 may use a chosen name and pronouns informally at school without parental consent under the rule effective 1 January 2025, while any change to formal school records still requires a parent's consent.

Residents who experience discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing or public and private accommodation may bring a complaint under the province's human rights legislation.

Resident students lived under the parental-consent rule from 1 July 2023 through 31 December 2024, an eighteen-month stretch in which teachers were barred from using a student's chosen name and pronouns without a parent's consent. That period is the most recent documented instance of the restriction; the current rule replaced it on 1 January 2025.

The policy's application clause binds parents, volunteers, student teachers and contract staff in the school environment, so resident adults present in schools are covered by the same name, pronoun and facilities rules as students.
outOfScopeNotes:
No New Brunswick provincial-jail placement rule for trans prisoners is documented in this inventory. Only the federal correctional policy is sourced here, and provincial correctional policies are noted to vary; whether a trans detainee in a New Brunswick provincial facility can request placement aligned with their gender identity is unresolved.

The procedure for changing a legal gender marker on New Brunswick identity or vital-records documents is not sourced in this inventory.

The inventory does not state whether the 1 January 2025 revision restored the extracurricular and sports wording dropped in 2023, or whether the gender-neutral bathroom requirement introduced in 2020 was altered by any revision.

No trans-specific violence or victimisation figure for New Brunswick is documented here, and no date for the most recent such incident in the province is available.
